facts.text: On May 18, 2005, Taiwan's Executive Yuan approved a plan to set up community care stations for older people.
The plan asked local groups to run the stations, with people from the neighborhood working as volunteers.
Community care stations offer healthy older people home visits, phone calls to check on them, health activities and meals.
There were 382 community care stations in 2005 and 1,969 in 2014.
By the end of May 2017 there were 2,710 community care stations in Taiwan.
By November 2025 Taiwan had 5,210 community care stations.
The stations aim to help older people grow old in their own neighborhoods.
At the stations, older people keep busy making friends, exercising, learning crafts and looking after their neighbors.
A survey cited by the health ministry found that 98.6% of people aged 65 and over had lost some teeth, 13.39 teeth on average.
Because of tooth problems, some older people find eating hard, which can lead to poor nutrition.
The Health Promotion Administration helps cooks at community dining stations choose, cut and cook food so that it is easy to chew and neither too hard nor too soft.
At one Taipei station, a soft egg tofu dish flavored with Pouchong tea became a favorite with older diners.
Older people at one station said they looked forward to every visit because they could enjoy tasty food and chat and laugh with friends over the meal.
Taiwan was expected to become a super-aged society in 2025, when people aged 65 and over would make up more than 20% of the population.
In December 2025 the health ministry said Taiwan had become a super-aged society.
In 2026 the government plans a version 2.0 of the community care stations and more help for older people who live alone, including visits, phone calls and meal delivery.
